subtype: Reading a partner's or roommate's unspoken needs [Interpreting]
passage: For a week, Kishore watched his hostel roommate Yash change. Yash's side of the room filled with unwashed mugs and crumpled notes. He stopped coming to the mess, answered in single words, and snapped when Kishore asked to borrow a charger. Kishore decided Yash needed space. So he stayed out late, studied in the library, and kept his music off. On Friday he came back to find Yash sitting on the floor in the dark. Kishore almost turned round and left again. Instead he sat on his own bed and asked, "Do you want company, or quiet? Either's fine." Yash was silent for a moment. Then: "Company, honestly. I thought you were avoiding me." Kishore felt his stomach drop. "I thought I was helping." They ordered parathas and Yash talked about his failed internship interview till two in the morning.

qa.q: What did Yash's side of the room fill with?
qa.a: Unwashed mugs and crumpled notes.

qa.q: What was Yash feeling during that week?
qa.a: He was low and lonely, and he felt Kishore was avoiding him; the clutter and snapping hinted at stress, and later he mentions a failed internship interview.

qa.q: What made the difference on Friday?
qa.a: Kishore asked plainly whether Yash wanted company or quiet, instead of acting on his guess.

qa.q: How did Kishore feel when he learned his guess had been wrong?
qa.a: He felt his stomach drop, likely guilty and surprised, because he had meant to help by staying away.

grounding: Shows a young adult reading a roommate's quietness and clutter as a need for space, and learning by asking that the guess was wrong.

subtype: Reading a partner's or roommate's unspoken needs [Interpreting]
passage:
Damini,
I'm leaving this note on the fridge because you've had your earphones in all week and I didn't want to interrupt.
I've noticed you coming home from the hospital and going straight to your room. The dishes piling up, which isn't like you. You snapped at me about the milk on Tuesday, which also isn't like you. So I've been keeping out of your way, thinking you need rest and space.
But I realised I'm only guessing. Maybe you want space. Maybe you want someone to make you dinner and not talk. Maybe you want to talk about something.
So: do you want company or quiet this week? Just write C or Q under this and I'll go with it. No explanation needed.
Rukmini

qa.q: Where does Damini come home from?
qa.a: From the hospital.

qa.q: What is Rukmini feeling while writing the note?
qa.a: Rukmini feels concerned about Damini and a bit unsure, having kept away while realising it was only a guess.

qa.q: Why is Rukmini's note a wise approach?
qa.a: It names the signs without blame, admits the reading may be wrong, and gives Damini an easy way to say what would help.

qa.q: How might Damini feel finding the note?
qa.a: Damini might feel noticed and cared for without pressure, since a single letter is enough and no explanation is needed.

grounding: Shows a young adult noticing a flatmate's signs of strain and checking whether the flatmate wants company or quiet rather than assuming.

subtype: Reading a partner's or roommate's unspoken needs [Interpreting]
passage: You're asking how Yamini and I survived her first year of night shifts? I'm Joseph, by the way, and I got it wrong at first. She'd come home at eight in the morning, drop her bag by the door, and go quiet. Not angry. Just quiet. I'd been waiting all night, so I'd follow her around, telling her about my day, making eggs, asking questions. She'd go stiff. I decided she was upset with me. For two weeks I sulked. Then one morning, she said, "Joe, I love you, but I can't hear words right now." So I asked her straight: "What do you want when you come home? Company, or quiet?" She thought about it. "Quiet for one hour. Then breakfast with you." So now I put the kettle on and read. At nine, she comes out and we eat together. Best hour of my day.

qa.q: When did Yamini come home from her night shifts?
qa.a: At eight in the morning.

qa.q: How did Joseph feel during those first two weeks?
qa.a: He felt hurt and sulked, believing Yamini was upset with him, when she was only exhausted.

qa.q: What small step helped Joseph and Yamini?
qa.a: Joseph asked directly whether she wanted company or quiet, and they agreed on an hour of quiet and then breakfast together.

qa.q: What was it like for Yamini when Joseph followed her around after a night shift?
qa.a: She was too exhausted to take in words, so the talking made her go stiff, even though she loves him.

grounding: Shows a young adult misreading a partner's quietness and learning to ask whether she wants company or quiet.

subtype: Giving feedback and rebuking [Expressing]
passage:
Monday. In the project meeting, Hemant's section of the report was missing again. Seema lost patience. "Hemant, you're dragging everyone down. Every week, same story." The room went silent. Hemant turned red and said, "Maybe if you explained things properly." They didn't speak for two days.
Wednesday. Seema caught him alone near the library. "I'm sorry about Monday. I shouldn't have said that in front of everyone." Hemant shrugged. She went on: "Your data section was due on the 10th and the 17th, and both came in after the group deadline. I'm worried about Friday's submission. Could you send me a draft by Thursday noon, even rough, so I can help?" Hemant was quiet, then said, "I've been stuck on the graphs. I didn't want to say."
Friday. His section came in Thursday at eleven, with a note: "Graphs okay now? Thanks for asking properly."

qa.q: When did Seema ask Hemant to send a draft?
qa.a: By Thursday noon.

qa.q: What was Hemant feeling after Seema's comment in Monday's meeting?
qa.a: He was embarrassed and defensive, turning red and snapping back that she hadn't explained properly.

qa.q: What changed in Seema's feedback on Wednesday, and why did it work?
qa.a: She gave it privately, apologised for the public rebuke, used specific dates and a clear suggestion, so Hemant felt safe to admit he was stuck.

qa.q: What would change if Seema had repeated the rebuke in Friday's meeting?
qa.a: Hemant would likely have become more defensive, and the problem with the graphs might never have come out.

grounding: Shows a young adult moving from a public rebuke to private, specific, respectful feedback with a suggestion, which works better.

subtype: Giving feedback and rebuking [Expressing]
passage: Raghav, you're a team lead now, so let your Noor didi tell you about my first month leading the design team at twenty-two. We had a junior, Imtiaz, who kept missing the colours in the client's brand guide. One day, in front of eight people, I held up his poster and said, "Did you even open the guide?" He stared at the table. After that he stopped asking me anything, and his work got worse, not better. My manager called me in. "What did you want him to learn?" she asked. "To check the guide." "Then tell him that, alone, with an example." So I did. I sat with Imtiaz and said, "On these two posters the blue was lighter than the guide's code. Could you keep the guide open next to your screen?" He nodded, and asked me three questions I'd never heard him ask. The next poster was perfect.

qa.q: How many people were there when young Noor held up the poster?
qa.a: Eight people.

qa.q: How did Imtiaz seem to feel after the public rebuke?
qa.a: He seemed ashamed and defensive, staring at the table and then stopping asking young Noor anything.

qa.q: What turning point in the story changed how young Noor gave feedback?
qa.a: Her manager's question about what she wanted Imtiaz to learn, which led her to give private, specific feedback with a suggestion.

qa.q: How did young Noor's manager see the public rebuke?
qa.a: She seemed to see it as missing the point, asking what Noor actually wanted Imtiaz to learn and pointing her to private, specific feedback.

grounding: Shows a young adult learning that private, specific and respectful feedback works better than a public rebuke.

subtype: Giving feedback and rebuking [Expressing]
passage: The pitch to the city council was in twenty minutes, and the office printer had jammed. Sarika was reprinting while flicking through Jagdish's slides on her phone. His slide six had a figure that contradicted slide two, and the council's engineer would spot it. Everyone was rushing around; the room was loud. She could have called across the room, "Jagdish, your numbers are wrong!" Instead she walked over and quietly said, "Two minutes? Just us." They stepped into the corridor. "Slide six says 40 buses, slide two says 34. The engineer will ask. I think 34 is right from the survey. Could you fix six before we go in?" Jagdish checked and groaned. "You're right. Thanks for not shouting it." He fixed it in a minute. In the meeting, the engineer did ask about the buses, and Jagdish answered without a stumble.

qa.q: How many buses did slide two say?
What was Jagdish feeling when he saw the mistake?
qa.a: He was dismayed, groaning at the error, and relieved and grateful that Sarika hadn't shouted it across the room.

qa.q: What made Sarika's feedback work under time pressure?
qa.a: She gave it privately and quickly, with the exact slides, the likely correct number and a clear request to fix it.

qa.q: What would change if Sarika had called out the error across the room?
qa.a: Jagdish might have felt embarrassed in front of everyone and become defensive, wasting precious minutes before the pitch.

grounding: Shows a young adult giving private, timely and specific feedback under pressure instead of a public rebuke.

subtype: Taking criticism without shrinking or bristling [Regulating]
passage: Nandini, you came to me upset about your manager's comments, so let your Kashish didi tell you about my first performance review, at twenty-three. My manager, Mr Rao, said my reports were "sloppy" and I "didn't take initiative". My face went hot. I wanted to argue: I'd stayed late every Friday for months! Instead I sat there saying, "Yes, sir, sorry, sir," and went home and cried, sure I was useless. I didn't sleep. Next day, my senior Lata said, "Did you ask him what he meant?" I hadn't. So I went back with a notebook. "Sir, which reports were sloppy?" He showed me two with wrong totals. Fair. "And initiative, can you give an example?" He couldn't really; he'd confused me with someone else. So I took the first point, fixed my checks, and told him politely the second didn't fit. He actually agreed.

qa.q: What did Mr Rao show young Kashish when asked which reports were sloppy?
qa.a: Two reports with wrong totals.

qa.q: How did young Kashish feel after the first review?
qa.a: She felt hurt and hopeless, crying at home and sure she was useless, instead of seeing what was fair and what wasn't.

qa.q: What turning point in the story helped Kashish learn from the review?
qa.a: Going back with a notebook and asking Mr Rao for examples, which separated the fair point about totals from the unfair one about initiative.

qa.q: How did Mr Rao respond when Kashish questioned the initiative comment?
qa.a: He couldn't give a real example and agreed, since he had confused her with someone else.

grounding: Shows a young adult moving from total self-blame to asking clarifying questions and separating fair criticism from unfair.

subtype: Taking criticism without shrinking or bristling [Regulating]
passage: The college drama script was due at the festival office by six, and it was already 4:45. Hemant, the director, flipped through Dhruv's pages in the noisy rehearsal hall. "The second scene drags. And honestly, the ending is cheesy." Dhruv felt the heat rise in his face. He'd spent three nights on that ending. His mouth opened to snap back. He shut it. With an hour left, a fight would waste the time. "Okay. Which part of scene two drags? Can you point to lines?" Hemant tapped a long speech. "Here. The mother repeats herself." Dhruv read it. Fair. He cut six lines. "And the ending, is it the words or the idea?" Hemant thought. "The idea's fine. The last line just spells it out." Dhruv crossed out the final line. It was stronger. They submitted at 5:52. The cheesy remark still stung, but the script was better.

qa.q: What time did they submit the script?
What was Dhruv feeling when Hemant called the ending cheesy?
qa.a: He felt stung and angry, the heat rising in his face after three nights of work; he wanted to snap back.

qa.q: What did Dhruv do that turned the criticism into something useful?
qa.a: He held back his reaction and asked clarifying questions about exact lines and whether the problem was the words or the idea.

qa.q: How might Hemant have seen Dhruv's questions?
qa.a: He probably saw them as a sign that Dhruv could take feedback, which made it easier to give a precise and fair answer.

grounding: Shows a young adult taking criticism under time pressure without bristling, asking clarifying questions and keeping what is useful.

subtype: Taking criticism without shrinking or bristling [Regulating]
passage: At the quarterly review in the Bengaluru office, Nazia went through Pranav's work. "Your client emails are excellent. Clear and polite. But your code reviews are slow, sometimes three days, and the team waits. And I've heard you're not a team player." Pranav's chest tightened. The last one felt unfair; he'd covered two colleagues' shifts last month. For a second he wanted to shrink into his chair and say sorry for everything. He breathed. "Thank you about the emails. On the code reviews, you're right. Can we agree on a target, maybe one day?" Nazia nodded. "On the team-player point, can you tell me where that came from? Last month I covered for Arjun and Sneha twice." Nazia paused and checked her notes. "Fair. That came from one person, and I hadn't looked into it. I'll take it out." Pranav left with one clear goal and his shoulders loose.

qa.q: How long do Pranav's code reviews sometimes take?
qa.a: Sometimes three days.

qa.q: What was Pranav feeling when Nazia said he wasn't a team player?
qa.a: He felt tense and hurt, his chest tightening, because the comment seemed unfair given he had covered colleagues' shifts.

qa.q: How did Pranav separate the fair criticism from the unfair one?
qa.a: He accepted the code review point and suggested a target, and calmly asked where the team-player comment came from, offering evidence.

qa.q: How did Nazia respond when Pranav questioned the team-player comment?
qa.a: She checked her notes, admitted it came from one person she hadn't looked into, and agreed to take it out.

grounding: Shows a young adult taking feedback without shrinking or bristling, asking questions and separating useful points from unfair ones.

subtype: Contempt and ridicule as warning signs [Interpreting]
passage: Jin had been with Oskar for a year in Stockholm when she started noticing something. At dinner with friends, when she told a story about her job at the museum, Oskar rolled his eyes and said, "Here comes another fascinating painting." Everyone laughed. At home, when she cried about her grandmother in Seoul, he sighed loudly: "Drama again." Each time, she laughed it off. But she'd started telling fewer stories. She felt smaller in her own flat. One evening, after he mimicked her accent in front of his cousins, she didn't laugh. At home she said, calmly, "When you mock me or roll your eyes when I talk, I feel disrespected. It keeps happening. I need it to stop." He scoffed. "You can't take a joke." That night Jin called her friend Mina and talked for an hour. The next week she booked a session with a counsellor at the student centre.

qa.q: What did Oskar say when Jin talked about her job at the museum?
qa.a: "Here comes another fascinating painting."

qa.q: What was Jin feeling as the mockery went on?
qa.a: She felt smaller and disrespected, telling fewer stories and laughing things off, until she no longer could.

qa.q: What steps did Jin take that were wise?
qa.a: She named the pattern calmly and set a limit, and when Oskar scoffed, she talked to a friend and booked a counsellor instead of trading insults.

qa.q: How did Oskar see Jin's request?
qa.a: He dismissed it, scoffing that she couldn't take a joke, which suggests he didn't see his mockery as disrespect.

grounding: Shows a young adult recognising repeated eye-rolls and mockery in a relationship as contempt, naming it, setting a limit and seeking help.

subtype: Contempt and ridicule as warning signs [Interpreting]
passage: In the Chennai design office, Neelam, the senior designer, had a habit. When Noor presented an idea, Neelam would smirk, glance at the others and say something like, "Cute. Very college project." Once she rolled her eyes so obviously that the intern giggled. Noor started saying less in meetings. She noticed her hands getting cold before every review. At first she wondered if she was being too sensitive. Then she began writing it down: dates, words, who was there. After the fourth time in a month, she asked Neelam for a word, privately. "When you call my ideas cute and roll your eyes in reviews, it feels like mockery. I'd like feedback on the work instead." Neelam laughed. "Relax." So Noor took her notes to her mentor, Mr Pillai. He read them, frowned and said, "This isn't about sensitivity. I'll raise it with HR and sit in on your next review."

qa.q: What did Neelam say about Noor's ideas?
qa.a: "Cute. Very college project."

qa.q: What was Noor feeling before reviews?
qa.a: She felt anxious, her hands getting cold before every review, and doubted herself, wondering if she was too sensitive.

qa.q: What steps did Noor take that others could copy?
qa.a: She wrote down the incidents, named the pattern calmly to Neelam, and when that failed, took her notes to her mentor for help.

qa.q: How did Mr Pillai respond when Noor showed him her notes?
qa.a: He took it seriously, said it wasn't about sensitivity, and promised to raise it with HR and sit in on her next review.

grounding: Shows a young adult recognising sneering and eye-rolls at work as disrespect, naming it calmly and seeking help rather than trading insults.

subtype: Contempt and ridicule as warning signs [Interpreting]
passage:
Santosh,
We've been friends since Class 6, so I'm going to say this straight, in writing, because when I try to say it out loud you laugh.
For a few months now, whenever I talk about my music, you roll your eyes or put on a squeaky voice and say, "Ooh, the artist." In front of the others too. At first I laughed along. Now I just stop talking. That's not how friends are supposed to feel with each other.
I'm not trying to start a fight or call you names. I'm naming what keeps happening. I'd like it to stop. If you think I've got it wrong, tell me; I'll listen.
If it keeps happening, I'll need to spend less time around you, and I really don't want that.
Still your friend,
Ujjwal

qa.q: How long have Ujjwal and Santosh been friends?
qa.a: Since Class 6.

qa.q: What is Ujjwal feeling about Santosh's mockery?
qa.a: Ujjwal feels hurt and small, having gone from laughing along to simply stopping talking, and is worried about losing the friendship.

qa.q: What makes Ujjwal's letter a wise response?
qa.a: It names the pattern calmly without insults, asks for it to stop, offers to listen, and sets a clear limit.

qa.q: How might Santosh see the squeaky voice compared with Ujjwal?
qa.a: Santosh may think it's harmless teasing, while for Ujjwal it has become mockery that makes Ujjwal stop sharing.

grounding: Shows a young adult recognising repeated mockery and eye-rolls as disrespect, naming it calmly and setting a limit.

subtype: Ultimatums in relationships [Mismatch]
passage:
"Delete Karan and Vikram from your phone," Siddharth said. "Or I'm done."
Shalini stared at him. "They're my lab partners."
"You're always laughing at their messages. If you loved me, you'd delete them."
"I do love you. And I'm not deleting my lab partners."
"Then choose."
"Sid, last month you said you'd leave if I went to my cousin's wedding without you. Now this."
"Because I care."
"Caring doesn't sound like 'choose or I leave' every few weeks."
He grabbed his jacket. "Fine. Call me when you've decided."
Shalini sat very still after he left, her hands shaking. Then she called her sister.
"Didi? Can you come over? I think something's not right."
"I'm coming now," Didi said. "Don't answer him till I'm there. We'll talk it through together."

qa.q: Who did Siddharth want Shalini to delete from her phone?
qa.a: Karan and Vikram.

qa.q: What was Shalini feeling after Siddharth left?
qa.a: She was shaken and scared, her hands shaking, and unsure what was happening, which is why she called her sister.

qa.q: Why was calling her sister a wise step?
qa.a: The ultimatums were repeated and controlling, not a fair boundary, so getting support from a trusted person helped Shalini think clearly and stay safe.

qa.q: How did Didi respond when Shalini called?
qa.a: She came straight away, told Shalini not to answer him until she arrived, and offered to talk it through together.

grounding: Shows a young adult recognising repeated ultimatums from a partner as pressure and control, and seeking support.

subtype: Ultimatums in relationships [Mismatch]
passage: The ultimatum I think about most came from my friend Irawati in our second year. I'm Rajni, and back then I was lying a lot. Small things: that I'd return her notes, that I'd be at her play, that I'd pay back the auto fare. One evening she sat me down. "Rajni, I love you. But if you lie to me one more time, I'm stepping back from this friendship." I was furious. I told her she was being dramatic, controlling. I cried to my roommate that night. But my roommate asked, "Is she telling you what to do, or telling you what she'll do?" That stopped me. Irawati wasn't ordering me around. She was saying what she needed to stay. I could choose. I chose to stop lying, clumsily at first. We're still friends. I've learned that some ultimatums are just someone's honest limit.

qa.q: What did Irawati say she would do if Rajni lied again?
qa.a: She would step back from the friendship.

qa.q: How did Rajni feel when Irawati gave the ultimatum?
qa.a: Rajni felt furious and hurt at first, calling Irawati dramatic and controlling, and cried to the roommate that night.

qa.q: What question helped Rajni see the ultimatum differently?
qa.a: The roommate's question: is she telling you what to do, or what she'll do? It showed Irawati was stating a boundary, leaving Rajni free to choose.

qa.q: How did Irawati likely see her own ultimatum?
qa.a: As an honest limit about what she needed to stay in the friendship after repeated lies, not as control.

grounding: Shows that some ultimatums state a real boundary and respect the other's choice, unlike pressure or control.

subtype: Ultimatums in relationships [Mismatch]
passage:
Counsellor's note, college wellbeing centre, Monday.
Anjali, a final-year student, came in today, very tense. Her father has told her that if she does not agree to marry a man the family has chosen by Diwali, she should "never come home again". Her mother has stopped speaking to her. She said, "Maybe he's just upset. Maybe it's normal." I asked whether she feels she has a real choice. She said no, and that she is afraid to go home for the holidays. We talked about the difference between a parent stating a limit and pressure that removes her choice and makes her afraid. I explained that she does not have to decide anything today. With her permission, I contacted the college's women's cell and a legal aid counsellor, and gave her the helpline number. She will stay in the hostel over the holiday. I will see her on Wednesday.
— Rekha

qa.q: When does Anjali's father want her to agree by?
qa.a: By Diwali.

qa.q: What was Anjali feeling during the session?
qa.a: She was tense and afraid to go home, and unsure whether her father's pressure was normal.

qa.q: What steps did the counsellor take that were wise?
qa.a: She explained Anjali didn't have to decide today, connected her with the women's cell and legal aid with her permission, gave the helpline and arranged for her to stay in the hostel.

qa.q: How does Rekha see the father's ultimatum?
qa.a: Rekha sees it as pressure that removes Anjali's choice and makes her afraid, not simply a parent stating a limit.

grounding: Shows a young adult facing a family ultimatum that is coercion, and a counsellor helping her find support where fear is present.

subtype: Appeals to emotion, authority and logic [Interpreting]
passage: Manjula, you asked me why I read every leaflet twice. Let your Raghav mama tell you. When I was twenty, a man came to our college with a "guaranteed rank" coaching course. He was very good. First he talked about our parents' sacrifices until half the room had tears in their eyes. Then he showed a photo of himself with a big officer: "Sir himself recommends us." Then he said, "Only ten seats left, and the offer ends tonight. You boys are clearly the smartest in this district." I wanted to sign right there. My friend Babloo nudged me. "Where are the results? Names? Numbers?" The man said, "Trust me." That was all. We didn't sign. Two months later, the course shut down. Emotion isn't always a trick, beti. But when it comes with hurry, fear and praise, and no proof, look twice.

qa.q: What did the man say about how many seats were left?
qa.a: Only ten seats left, and the offer ends tonight.

qa.q: How did young Raghav feel during the salesman's talk?
qa.a: He was moved and eager, wanting to sign right there, after the talk about parents' sacrifices and the flattery.

qa.q: What turning point in the story stopped Raghav from signing?
qa.a: His friend Babloo asked for results, names and numbers, and the man could only say "Trust me."

qa.q: How did the room react to the part about parents' sacrifices?
qa.a: Half the room had tears in their eyes, showing how strongly the emotional appeal worked on them.

grounding: Shows a young adult learning to spot emotional, authority and flattery appeals with urgency, and to ask for evidence.

subtype: Appeals to emotion, authority and logic [Interpreting]
passage: It was the night before Reena's own exam when Chinmay messaged her. "Reena, you're the only one who can save me. My assignment is due at nine tomorrow. Please write it? You're a genius, seriously. If I fail, my dad will kill me." Reena stared at the phone. Her chest tightened. She did like Chinmay, and she felt awful imagining him in trouble. But she noticed how the message was built: flattery, fear, a deadline in twelve hours. And her own exam was at ten. She typed slowly. "I'm sorry you're stressed. I can't write it for you, and I have my exam. But I can send you my notes on the topic and you can call me for fifteen minutes at seven." Chinmay replied, "Fine, thanks." At seven he did call, with questions. She answered, then went back to her own books.

qa.q: When was Chinmay's assignment due?
qa.a: At nine tomorrow.

qa.q: What was Reena feeling when she read Chinmay's message?
qa.a: She felt tense and torn, her chest tightening, because she cared about him and felt awful, but her own exam was the next day.

qa.q: What helped Reena respond wisely?
qa.a: She noticed the flattery, fear and deadline in the message, said no to writing it, and offered smaller help that fit her own time.

qa.q: How might Chinmay have felt when Reena said no?
qa.a: He may have felt disappointed, replying only "Fine, thanks", but he still called and got useful help.

grounding: Shows a young adult noticing flattery, fear and urgency in a personal request and weighing it before acting.

subtype: Appeals to emotion, authority and logic [Interpreting]
passage: At the Mumbai mall, two stalls stood side by side. At the first, a volunteer from an animal shelter showed Anjali and Tejas photos of rescued dogs. "We feed eighty dogs a day. Here's our last year's report and the vet's details. Donate if you want; no pressure." Anjali's eyes softened. At the second stall, a man in a crisp shirt stopped them with a loud voice. "Water in your building is poisoning your kids. Scientists agree. Our filter, today only, half price. Families like yours deserve the best." Tejas's face went pale. "Poison? Should we call Mummy?" Anjali pulled him aside. "Wait. The dog people gave a report. This man gave 'scientists agree' and 'today only'. No name. No test." Tejas breathed out. They took the shelter's leaflet and walked past the filter stall. At home, they looked up the building's last water test. It was fine.

qa.q: How many dogs does the shelter say it feeds a day?
qa.a: Eighty dogs a day.

qa.q: What was Anjali feeling at the shelter stall?
qa.a: Her eyes softened, suggesting she felt moved and warm toward the rescued dogs, without feeling pushed.

qa.q: How did Anjali tell the two appeals apart?
qa.a: The shelter's emotional appeal came with a report and vet details and no pressure, while the filter pitch used fear, vague authority, flattery and urgency without proof.

qa.q: What would change if Tejas had acted on his fear at the stall?
qa.a: He might have rushed into buying the filter today only, without checking the building's water test, which turned out to be fine.

grounding: Shows a young adult weighing appeals to emotion and authority, trusting evidence and scrutinising urgency, fear and flattery.

subtype: Negotiating shared living or study arrangements [Expressing]
passage:
Sunday night.
Jeevan and I finally had the chore talk. For weeks I'd been saying "you never clean the kitchen" and Jeevan saying "you're always nagging". Positions, positions.
Today I tried what Ma'am said in the negotiation class: ask what each person actually needs. So I asked. Turns out Jeevan hates doing dishes at night because the early shift starts at six. What I need is a clean kitchen before I cook dinner at eight. Different things!
So we worked it out: Jeevan does the dishes in the morning, after tea, and takes the bins out. I do the evening wipe-down and the bathroom on Saturdays. We split the cleaning supplies half and half.
Then Jeevan said, "Let's write it down, so we don't fight later." We stuck it on the fridge with the pineapple magnet. First time in a month I'm going to bed not annoyed.
— Ishita

qa.q: Where did Ishita and Jeevan stick the agreement?
qa.a: On the fridge with the pineapple magnet.

subtype: Negotiating shared living or study arrangements [Expressing]
passage: In their two-room house in Nagaur, Preeti and her brother Chetan shared the only table with a working light. Both had board exams in a month, and every evening turned into shouting. "I need the table!" "No, I do!" Their mother finally sat them down. "Stop saying who needs the table. Tell me what you need to study." Preeti thought. "I need quiet to learn my science diagrams. After ten the street goes quiet." Chetan said, "I need the light for writing maths. I can't do it on the floor. But I'm dead tired by ten." Preeti blinked. "So you take the table from six to ten, and I take it after?" "And you use the charpai for reading diagrams before ten," Chetan said. They wrote the timetable in chalk on the wall beside the calendar. For the next month, nobody shouted about the table.

subtype: Sharing memories and identity [Expressing]
passage: The first time I really told anyone about my family was in a college ice-breaker I was dreading. I'm Nilesh. We had to share one story from home. Ankita went first and talked about her grandmother's pickle shop in Nagpur, and everyone laughed. When it was my turn, I told them how my great-grandfather walked from Sindh to Mumbai in 1947 with only a copper pot, and how that pot sits on our shelf now. The room went quiet, then people asked questions. It felt good to be known a little. But when someone asked, "So what caste are you, then?", I felt my shoulders go tight. I said, "I'd rather not get into that." Ankita changed the subject for me without making a fuss. Later I told her about some harder parts of that migration story, the parts I hadn't shared with the whole room. That was my choice, and it felt right.

qa.a: On their shelf.

qa.q: How did Nilesh feel when asked about caste?
qa.a: Nilesh felt uncomfortable and guarded, shoulders going tight, and chose not to answer.

qa.q: What did Ankita do that helped?
qa.a: She changed the subject quietly without making a fuss, respecting Nilesh's choice not to share.

qa.q: How might the person who asked about caste have seen the question?
qa.a: They may have thought it was just curiosity, not realising it pushed for private details Nilesh didn't want to share.

grounding: Shows a young adult sharing family history to be known while choosing what to keep private, and a friend respecting that.

Mentor's note, first-year orientation week, Thursday.
At our "Where I come from" evening, Pranav, a first-year, shared the story of his family's small tea stall in Siliguri and how his mother ran it alone after his father left. The group listened closely. Two students thanked him afterwards. Then one of the others asked, loudly, "And are you seeing anyone? You never talk about that." Pranav smiled tightly and said, "Some things I keep for later." The student pushed: "Come on, we're all sharing." I stepped in and said that everyone chooses what they share and when, and nobody owes the group private details. Pranav looked relieved. Afterwards I told him privately that he had handled it well and that my door is open anytime, for anything. I've also reminded the whole group in our chat that "sharing" nights are about choice.
— Pallavi

Irawati and I finally went for that long walk by the lake. She told me about growing up in Pune, her grandfather's bookshop, how she learned Marathi and Kannada at the same time. So I told her about Eid at my Nani's house in Hyderabad, the thirty cousins, and the haleem my Ammi still makes every year. It felt so nice to be known like that.
Then she asked, "Do you wear a hijab at home?" I don't mind that question. But she followed with, "What do your parents think about you living alone?", and I noticed I didn't want to answer that one yet. There's a story there, and I don't know her well enough.
So I said, "That's a long one. Another time?" She just said, "Of course," and asked about the haleem recipe. I think we're going to be real friends.

She said she felt the same about her English, and told me how kids teased her accent in school. A few weeks later, I told her a little more: that my father hadn't wanted me to study so far from home. She told me about her parents' divorce. Each time, it felt like we were both stepping forward together. I did once try to tell a girl from my lab everything about my family on the second day we met, and I felt so exposed afterwards that I avoided her for a week.

In today's small-group session, Jatin shared a great deal very quickly: his parents' fights, his breakup, a time he failed a year. The group was kind but quiet; no one shared much back. Payal, the peer mentor, noticed Jatin's face change afterwards. He went red and kept apologising, "Sorry, too much." After the session she sat with him. She told him nothing he said was wrong to feel, but that trust usually grows when people share bit by bit and see if others share back. She suggested he start with smaller things next week and watch how the group responds. Jatin said he felt embarrassed but also relieved someone had explained. I agree with Payal's approach and will check in with Jatin next week. I've also reminded mentors to open each session with lighter sharing before deeper topics.

Three months with Nitin. Tonight on the terrace I told him the thing I haven't told anyone outside my family: that I stammered badly till I was fourteen and used to hide in the school toilet during roll call. My heart was thumping. I kept watching his face.
He didn't make a joke. He just listened. Then, after a while, he said he'd never told anyone that his older brother used to hit him, and that it's why he goes quiet when people shout. I didn't know that. I held his hand.
It feels different now, closer, like we both put something on the table. I'm glad I didn't tell him this in our first week, when I almost did. I don't think either of us would have been ready.
— Chandrika

subtype: Dry wit and comic understatement [Expressing]
passage: I still laugh about the night our hostel flooded in Chennai. I'm Yusuf. The rain came through the window at 2 a.m., and by morning there was water up to our ankles, my mattress floating, and my laptop sitting on top of the cupboard where I'd flung it. My roommate Varun, standing in the doorway in his shorts, looked at the whole mess and said, "It's slightly damp." I lost it. I laughed so much I sat down in the water. And somehow, after that, it didn't feel like a disaster. We fished out our books, hung the clothes on the stair railings, and I kept saying "slightly damp" all day. The warden didn't find it as funny. When she asked how our room was, Varun said, "Bit breezy," and she just stared at him. She hadn't seen the room. We had to show her.

qa.a: Yusuf could see the real mess, so the understatement read as coping; the warden hadn't seen the room, so she didn't get the irony.

qa.a: She just stared, probably confused or unamused, since she didn't know the true scale of the flood.

Coach's note, college hockey team, after Saturday's match.
We lost 0–6 to the university team. It was a hard afternoon; the boys were quiet in the dressing room, heads down. Anirban, our goalkeeper, who had faced about thirty shots, took off his pads, looked around and said, "Well. Not our finest hour." There was a pause, and then Madhav laughed, then everyone did. I watched the room loosen. Anirban's understatement worked because everyone knew exactly how bad it had been; it said "we all saw it, and we're still here". I noticed he was the one who had most reason to feel low, and he chose that line. Later, in the bus, I asked him privately how he was really doing. He said, "Honestly? Gutted. But I didn't want everyone sulking." I told him I appreciated it, and that he could be gutted with me too. We'll review the match on Tuesday.
— Coach Mehra

Monday night.
Interview day. The scooter broke down in the pouring rain two kilometres from the office. I pushed it into a petrol pump, got into an auto, the auto got a flat tyre, and I walked the last bit with my file inside my kurta so the certificates wouldn't get soaked. Walked in dripping, eleven minutes late.
Afterwards I sat in a café and texted Yash: "Not my best day." Yash replied: "Uh oh. How not-best? Scale of 1 to monsoon?" I laughed for the first time all day. Told the whole story. Yash said, "You still went in, though. Dripping. That's a story they'll remember."
And the funny thing is, the panel did smile when I said, "Sorry, the weather had other plans." One of them said, "Clearly." Waiting to hear back. Changing into dry socks now.
— Vasudha
